GitHub Copilot plans comparison — key differences trainers must explain:
Free/Pro: Public code filter, personal use, no content exclusions, no IP indemnity

Custom agents: defined as .agent.md files in .github/agents/ — teams can create specialized agents for specific workflows

GitHub Copilot Spaces: collaborative coding environments
GitHub Spark: rapid prototyping from natural language

info.label: Trainer Focus
items: Walk through the inbound and outbound data flow step by step

info.label: Talking Points
items: INBOUND FLOW — How your prompt becomes a suggestion:
Step 1 — Secure Prompt Transmission: User prompt sent over HTTPS to GitHub Copilot servers
Step 2 — Context Gathering: Copilot collects code before/after cursor, filename, file type, adjacent open tabs, project structure, language/framework info, and uses Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) technique
Step 3 — Proxy Filter: Prompt passes to proxy server in GitHub-owned Azure tenant; blocks prompt injection and manipulation attempts
Step 4 — Toxicity Filtering: Content filtering blocks hate speech, offensive language, personal data (names, addresses, IDs)
Step 5 — Code Generation with LLM: Filtered prompt passed to large language models for code suggestion generation
OUTBOUND FLOW — How suggestions are validated:
Step 6 — Post-Processing: Toxicity filter removes harmful content; proxy applies quality/security/ethics checks; checks for XSS, SQL injection vulnerabilities
Step 7 — Public Code Matching (optional): Admin-configurable filter prevents suggestions >150 characters that match public GitHub code — required for IP indemnity
Step 8 — Suggestion Delivery: Only suggestions passing all filters are delivered to user
Step 9 — Feedback Loop: Copilot learns from accepted, modified, and rejected suggestions
Key privacy points: Business/Enterprise data is not used for model training; prompts are not stored beyond the session; all processing happens on Azure infrastructure
LLM Limitations to discuss: potential for incorrect logic, security vulnerabilities, bias from training data, hallucination of non-existent APIs, outdated patterns

info.label: Talking Points

Microsoft/GitHub Six Principles of Responsible AI:
1. Fairness — AI systems should treat all people fairly; use diverse training data, detect bias, monitor across user segments
2. Reliability & Safety — AI must operate reliably, respond safely to unexpected conditions, resist harmful manipulation
3. Privacy & Security — Respect user privacy: obtain consent, collect only needed data, anonymize via pseudonymization/aggregation, encrypt with HSMs and secure vaults
4. Inclusiveness — AI systems must empower everyone regardless of ability, language, or geography; support screen readers, diverse dialects, offline use
5. Transparency — Explain how systems operate, justify design choices, be honest about limitations, enable auditability with logging and reporting
6. Accountability — AI creators must be responsible for system operation; continuous monitoring, risk mitigation, clear governance frameworks
Responsible AI is an approach to developing, assessing, and deploying AI in a safe, trustworthy, and ethical way — keeping people and their goals at the center
Practical application: always validate Copilot suggestions for correctness, security, and alignment with project requirements before accepting

info.label: Talking Points
items: The 4 S's of Prompt Engineering (from Microsoft Learn):
Single — Focus on one well-defined task or question per prompt
Specific — Make instructions explicit and detailed for precise suggestions
Short — Keep prompts concise while being specific — balance clarity without overloading
Surround — Use descriptive filenames and keep related files open to provide rich context
Learning approaches for Copilot:
Zero-shot: No examples — rely on Copilot's training alone; ideal for common patterns (e.g., temperature conversion from a comment)
One-shot: Single example to guide Copilot for context-aware, consistent implementations
Few-shot: Multiple examples to balance unpredictability with precision; excels at handling edge cases
Advanced prompting techniques:
Role prompting: Instruct Copilot to 'Act as a security expert' or 'Act as a performance optimization expert' for domain-specific output
Chain prompting: Build iterative conversations — Turn 1: Create function → Turn 2: Add error handling → Turn 3: Add tests → Turn 4: Add docs
Cues: Provide 'jumpstart' prefixes that direct Copilot's output format and direction
Best practices from Microsoft Learn:
Be Specific — leave as little to interpretation as possible
Be Descriptive — use analogies where helpful
Double Down — repeat key instructions before and after primary content
Order Matters — instruction placement affects output (recency bias)
Give the model an 'out' — include fallback like 'respond with not found if answer is not present'
Context sources Copilot uses: code before/after cursor, filename and type, open tabs in editor, project structure and file paths, programming languages and frameworks
Managing long conversations: summarize context when chats grow long, reset for new features, use concise references instead of repeating full implementations

info.label: Talking Points
items: Content Exclusions (Business/Enterprise only):
Admins can configure Copilot to ignore specific files or repositories
Excluded files: no completions available, cannot be referenced in chat or inline chat, content not included in suggestions for other files
Configured at repository or organization level
VS Code and Visual Studio both respect exclusion rules from the root repository
Matching Public Code filter:
Identifies and filters suggestions >150 characters matching publicly available code on GitHub
Essential for maintaining code originality and reducing compliance risk
Organization admins (Business/Enterprise): can block for all members — required for IP indemnity activation
Personal users (Free/Pro): can toggle Allow/Block in Settings → Copilot → Features → Privacy
If seat is org-provided, toggle may be locked to organization policy
IP Indemnity (Business/Enterprise only):
Provides legal protection against intellectual property claims from Copilot suggestions
Requirement: Matching public code setting must be set to 'Block'
GitHub assumes legal responsibility if a suggestion is challenged as infringing third-party IP
Covered by GitHub's Data Protection Agreement (DPA)
GitHub Copilot Trust Center provides full details on security, privacy, compliance
Audit Logs:
Available on Business/Enterprise plans for tracking Copilot usage
Admins can utilize audit log events for compliance monitoring
REST API available for managing subscriptions and usage metrics
Ownership of outputs: generated code suggestions — understand limitations and legal considerations
Duplication detection and security warnings: enable to catch vulnerable coding patterns

info.label: Talking Points
items: Measurement Framework — four stages:
1. Evaluation: focus on leading indicators — developer satisfaction, task completion rates; track Daily Active Users, Acceptance Rate, Lines of Code Accepted
2. Adoption: monitor productivity metrics and enablement indicators; identify training needs via API insights
3. Optimization: fine-tune impact on organizational goals — reduce time-to-market, improve code quality
4. Sustained efficiency: continuously evaluate as organization evolves; ongoing monitoring and adjustment
REST API for usage metrics: GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/usage — provides daily breakdown of suggestions, acceptances, active users by editor and language
Also available at team and organization level: /team/{team_slug}/copilot/usage and /orgs/{org}/copilot/usage
GitHub Copilot Developer Survey:
Short-form: every 2 weeks — overall satisfaction, challenges, time saved
Long-form: every 4 weeks — deeper analysis of impact on team dynamics, detailed usage patterns
Key questions: 'How would you feel if you could no longer use GitHub Copilot?', 'I complete tasks faster / write better quality code / enjoy coding more'
Anonymize responses, track trends over time in BI tools
Research results: developers using Copilot completed tasks 55% faster and had 78% higher success rate (GitHub research study)
